parts.title: Getting up at five
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
Last autumn, I decided to change my routine and get up at five every morning. Everyone told me that the early hours are the best time to work, and I wanted to see if it was true.

The first week was a disaster. I set my alarm for 5 a.m., but every morning I turned it off and went back to sleep. In the end, my sister suggested a trick: she told me to put the alarm on the other side of the room. When I had to get out of bed to stop the noise, I was awake.

After two weeks, it became easier. At that time of day, the world is silent, and I could write, go for a run or just have breakfast in peace. My neighbours were still asleep, my phone was quiet, and nobody needed anything from me.

However, there was a price. I was so tired in the evenings that I could not stay awake after nine o'clock, so I stopped seeing my friends on weekdays. After two months, I changed my plan to six o'clock. It is not as magical as five, but I still have the quiet time, and I have my evenings back.

questions.prompt: Why did the writer try getting up at five?
options: To test what people told her
Because her job began very early
Because her sister asked her to
questions.explanation: People told her that early hours are the best time to work, and she wanted to see if it was true.

questions.prompt: What went wrong in the first week?
options: She turned off her alarm each day
She could not find her alarm clock
She was ill for several days
questions.explanation: She turned off the alarm every morning and went back to sleep.

questions.prompt: How did she solve the problem?
options: By going to bed much earlier
By using an alarm on her phone
questions.explanation: Her sister told her to put the alarm on the other side of the room.

questions.prompt: What did she like about the early hours?
questions.explanation: The world was silent, and nobody needed anything from her.

questions.prompt: Why did she change to six o'clock?
options: Her sister got up later than she did
The mornings were too dark to run
She was too tired at night
questions.explanation: She was too tired to stay awake after nine, so she stopped seeing her friends.

parts.title: The night bus driver
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There is one extra sentence.
parts.passage:
At eleven o'clock at night, when most people are going to bed, Mina Torres is starting work. She drives the number 24 night bus through the city, and she has been doing it for eight years. [1] Her family says that she lives 'upside down', but she says she loves it.

Mina sleeps from nine in the morning until four in the afternoon. [2] She puts thick curtains on her bedroom window and turns off her phone, so that nothing can wake her. After she gets up, she cooks dinner for her children, who are just coming home from school.

Her passengers are very different from those in the day. [3] Some are nurses going home after a long shift, and others are students who have missed the last train. 'A few of them fall asleep and miss their stop,' she laughs. [4] She always checks the seats at the end of the line before she leaves.

The worst part is winter, when the weather is cold and the streets are empty. [5] But Mina says that she would not change her job. 'At night, the city belongs to us,' she says.
sentences: Sometimes the heating on the bus breaks, and everyone feels cold until the end of the line.
There are far fewer of them, and they are usually tired and quiet.
She learned to drive when she was twenty, in her father's old truck.
It is not an easy timetable, because she finishes at seven in the morning.
Others forget things, such as umbrellas, bags and sometimes even shoes.
Getting enough sleep in the daytime is difficult, so she has learned a few tricks.

gaps.explanation: The sentence explains that her timetable is hard, and the next sentence says that her family thinks she lives upside down.
The sentence says that daytime sleep is difficult, and the next sentence describes her tricks with curtains and her phone.
The sentence says that night passengers are fewer and quieter, and the next sentence gives examples of who they are.
The sentence says that other passengers forget things, which is why she checks the seats at the end of the line.
The sentence gives another winter problem, and the next sentence says that Mina would still not change her job.

parts.title: Sleeping better
parts.instructions: Choose the correct word for each gap.
parts.passage:
Many teenagers do not get enough sleep, which can make it hard to [1] attention at school. Experts say that young people need about nine hours a night. One of the easiest ways to improve your sleep is to go to bed [2] the same time every evening. Try to avoid screens for an hour before bed, because the light from them tells your brain that it is still daytime. A warm shower or a quiet book can help you [3] down.

It is also a good idea to keep your room cool and dark. Finally, do not drink coffee or cola in the evening, because they [4] caffeine, which keeps you awake. If you still cannot sleep after twenty minutes, get up and do something [5], like listening to soft music, until you feel [6].

questions.prompt: Gap 1
questions.explanation: The fixed expression is "pay attention".

questions.prompt: Gap 2
questions.explanation: We say "at the same time".

questions.prompt: Gap 3
questions.explanation: To "wind down" means to relax after a busy day.

questions.prompt: Gap 4
questions.explanation: Coffee and cola contain caffeine.

questions.prompt: Gap 5
questions.explanation: The adjective "relaxing" describes the activity, such as soft music.

questions.prompt: Gap 6
questions.explanation: You feel sleepy before you fall asleep.

parts.title: A message about my day
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage:
Hi Jonas,
Thanks for your email. You asked [1] my daily routine, so here it is! On school days, I get up at half past six and [2] a quick shower. Then I have breakfast with my brother, and we catch the bus at ten to eight. I usually get home [3] four o'clock. After that, I do my homework, and [4] the weather is good, I go for a run before dinner. We eat at seven, and I am usually in bed [5] ten. At the weekends, I sleep much later! What time do you [6] up on Saturdays?
Write soon,
Hanne

gaps.explanation: We say "have a shower" or "take a shower".
She usually gets home at or by four o'clock.
The run depends on the weather, so "if" or "when" fits.
"In bed by ten" means no later than ten, and "at ten" is also possible.
"Get up" or "wake up" asks about the time you leave your bed.

parts.title: A sleep workshop
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note with one word.

turns.speaker: leona
turns.text: Good evening, and welcome to our sleep workshop at the Riverside Health Centre. My name is Leona, and I'm a nurse here. Today I'll give you five simple ideas for better sleep. First, keep the same bedtime every night, because your body likes routine. Second, make your bedroom dark. Even a small light from a phone can wake you. Third, don't eat a big meal late in the evening. A light snack, such as a banana, is fine. Fourth, take some exercise during the day, but not in the last two hours before bed. Finally, try writing down your worries on a piece of paper, so that you don't think about them in bed. At the end, you will receive a free leaflet, and next Tuesday we will have a second workshop about how children sleep. There is tea and coffee in the hall, but I suggest that you avoid the coffee!

gaps.explanation: Leona says to keep the same bedtime every night.
Her second idea is to make the bedroom dark.

gaps.prompt: A light snack, such as a ___, is fine
gaps.explanation: She says that a light snack such as a banana is fine.

gaps.prompt: Do not exercise in the last ___ hours before bed
gaps.explanation: She says no exercise in the last two hours before bed.

gaps.prompt: Write down your worries on a piece of ___
gaps.explanation: She suggests writing worries on a piece of paper.

gaps.prompt: Next Tuesday there is a workshop about how ___ sleep
gaps.explanation: The second workshop is about how children sleep.

parts.title: A sleep scientist
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: ivor
turns.text: With me today is Dr Elowen Grey, who studies sleep. Elowen, why do we sleep?

turns.speaker: elowen
turns.text: Nobody knows everything yet, but we know that during sleep the brain sorts out the memories of the day. It's like tidying a room.

turns.speaker: ivor
turns.text: How much sleep do we need?

turns.speaker: elowen
turns.text: It varies. Most adults need seven or eight hours, but teenagers need nine. Many of them get only six, which is a problem.

turns.speaker: ivor
turns.text: Is it true that we can catch up on sleep at the weekend?

turns.speaker: elowen
turns.text: Only partly. Sleeping late on Sunday helps a little, but it also makes it harder to fall asleep that night.

turns.speaker: ivor
turns.text: What about naps?

turns.speaker: elowen
turns.text: A short nap of twenty minutes in the afternoon is excellent. If it's longer than an hour, you wake up feeling worse than before.

turns.speaker: ivor
turns.text: Do you have trouble sleeping yourself?

turns.speaker: elowen
turns.text: Sometimes. When I travel to another time zone, I wake up in the middle of the night. I go outside into the sunlight in the morning, which helps my body to adjust.

turns.speaker: ivor
turns.text: Finally, what's your best tip?

turns.speaker: elowen
turns.text: Switch off your phone an hour before bed. It's the simplest change, and people notice the difference within a week.
